title: How high does it get?

prereqs.why: The identity in distribution between the running maximum and the absolute value is the whole of the calculation.
B(1) is standard normal, which is what turns the answer into a number.
The symmetry of the normal distribution is what collapses the two tails into one.

statement:
Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion and let

$$M(t) = \max\{\,B(s) : 0 \le s \le t\,\}$$

be its running maximum.

The reflection principle says that reflecting the path after it first
reaches a level $a$ gives another Brownian motion, and the consequence is

$$M(t) \ \overset{d}{=}\ \bigl|B(t)\bigr| .$$

Since $B(1) \sim N(0,1)$, find $\P\bigl(M(1) \ge 1\bigr)$.

Give the answer as a decimal to **three decimal places**; it is checked to
within $\pm 0.001$. You may use $\Phi(1) = 0.8413$, where $\Phi$ is the
standard normal distribution function.
hints: Rewrite the question using the identity: $\P(M(1) \ge 1) = \P(|B(1)| \ge 1)$.
$|Z| \ge 1$ means $Z \ge 1$ or $Z \le -1$, and those two events are disjoint.
The standard normal is symmetric about zero, so the two tails have the same probability.

payload.prompt: The probability that Brownian motion reaches level 1 at some point before time 1.
payload.label: $\P\bigl(M(1) \ge 1\bigr) \approx$
payload.syntax: A decimal, to three decimal places. Checked to within 0.001.
